content.title: About
content.content: Snapper (also known as red sea bass) is a marine fish that inhabits tropical and subtropical waters. Wild‑caught snapper is flash‑frozen right after harvest, preserving its natural flavor, texture, and nutrients. The fish has firm white flesh, a mildly sweet taste, and a moderately dense structure, making it ideal for grilling, baking, and sautéing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Snapper is commonly found around coral reefs and island coastlines.
Wild‑caught fish is considered more environmentally sustainable than farmed fish because it does not require intensive feed or chemical additives.
Snapper retains its aroma well when cooked at high temperatures.
In some cultures snapper is a prized delicacy served at festive occasions.
Freezing at -18 °C or lower retains over 90 % of the fish’s vitamins and minerals.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Snapper provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: It contains less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, most of which are polyunsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Wild snapper supplies EPA and DHA omega‑3 fatty acids that support brain function and cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The fish is rich in vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Snapper provides selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, contributing to antioxidant protection and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including snapper.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: As with many larger predatory fish, snapper can contain trace amounts of mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Improper storage
items.content: If thawed fish is left at room temperature for more than 2 hours, bacterial growth risk increases.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Snapper can be pan‑seared, baked, grilled, or steamed. Before cooking, rinse the fillets under cold water and pat dry with paper towels. When baking, add lemon, herbs, and a drizzle of olive oil to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen snapper in a freezer at -18 °C or lower. After thawing, use within 1–2 days and store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. Do not refreeze.
